turns.text: I’m giving the workshop agent one tiny printer job, and one instruction: put it at the end of the queue. Nothing clever. Nothing urgent. Nothing gets promoted.
A restrained request. This is growth.
It moved a printer job ahead of three of my projects last time. I would like to know whether that was a weird one-off or whether the agent thinks every plastic doodad deserves executive parking.
Then do not give it a vague instruction and act surprised when it improvises. What, precisely, did you tell it?
“Add this job after the existing jobs. Do not change their order.” That’s it. One little test before I let it touch anything more important.
Better. If the queue changes, we have a specific problem. If it does not, we have learned one instruction can survive contact with the agent.
And if it moves my projects again, we learn the printer has a very confident new manager.
Do not reward bad behavior with a title.
The job is in the queue. My three projects are still where they were. So far, the agent has behaved like a reasonable workshop assistant.
So far is doing considerable work in that sentence.
Fair. I’m leaving the queue alone and checking it again before anything prints. Apparently the exciting part of automation is watching it politely not ruin your afternoon.
